title: Gegenpressing: How Jurgen Klopp's Idea Changed the Way Football Is Played
summary: The idea of winning the ball back immediately after losing it — counter-pressing, or gegenpressing — has become one of football's dominant tactical concepts. We trace how it developed, why it works, and how it has spread across the game.
content:
In 2011, Jurgen Klopp said something that became one of football's most quoted tactical observations: "The best moment to win the ball is immediately after you've lost it. The opponent is not organised yet, their players are still moving forward. If we press immediately, we can win it back in a dangerous position."

This was not an entirely new idea. Pressing — the collective effort to win the ball back quickly — had been part of football for decades. But Klopp's Borussia Dortmund systematised it, executed it at a pace and intensity that had rarely been seen, and demonstrated that high-intensity collective pressing could dismantle even well-organised opponents.

What Gegenpressing Actually Is

Gegenpressing (German for counter-pressing) is the immediate collective effort to win the ball back within seconds of losing it. When Dortmund — and later Klopp's Liverpool — lost possession, the nearest players did not retreat to their defensive shape. They pressed the ball immediately, as a coordinated unit, trying to win it back before the opponent could establish any rhythm.

The logic is elegant: in the moment after losing the ball, the opponent's players are often not in their ideal positions. The player who just won the ball may be facing the wrong way. Teammates are still in transition. If you press immediately and collectively, you catch them in this moment of disorganisation.

Why It Works

The effectiveness of gegenpressing comes from its combination of physical and cognitive demands on the opponent. Physically, players under immediate pressure after winning the ball have less time to control, look up, and pass accurately. Cognitively, the constant threat of immediate pressing creates anxiety — players hurry decisions, make errors, play backwards when they should play forward.

At Liverpool under Klopp, the pressing was so intense that some opponents effectively gave up trying to play out from the back. They kicked long rather than face the immediate press of Firmino, Mane, and Salah.

Gegenpressing is the best playmaker in the world. If you win the ball high up the pitch, you're already in a dangerous position. You don't need to build an attack — the press has already built it for you.

The Physical Cost

The obvious limitation of high-intensity pressing is that it is enormously physically demanding. Covering the distances required, maintaining the intensity across 90 minutes, recovering quickly enough to press again after a sprint — this requires exceptional fitness levels and careful squad rotation.

Klopp's teams typically dropped in intensity in the final third of the season when fatigue accumulated. Managing the physical demands of gegenpressing across a long campaign is one of the key tactical challenges for managers who adopt the approach.

The Spread of the Idea

Gegenpressing is now everywhere in football. Pep Guardiola's Manchester City press intensely. Thomas Tuchel's teams have always pressed. Mikel Arteta's Arsenal built their recent success on a pressing foundation. The idea that winning the ball back immediately is preferable to retreating into shape has become mainstream in elite football.

The question for the next generation of coaches is what comes after pressing — because as every team presses, the advantage of pressing diminishes, and the game will evolve again.
